title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes Euler's 'first class' and begins the 'second class' in his classification of integrals ∫Z dx by the order of the resulting Euler–Lagrange equation. In modern terms, write p = y', dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp, so M = Z_x, N = Z_y, P = Z_p.

First class (completed here). For a Lagrangian affine in p, L = Z(x,y) + 𝔷(x,y)·p with d𝔷 = 𝔐dx + 𝔑dy, the Euler–Lagrange equation L_y − d/dx L_p = 0 becomes N + 𝔑p − (𝔐 + 𝔑p) = 0. The p-terms cancel, leaving 0 = N − 𝔐, i.e. Z_y − 𝔷_x = 0. This is a finite (algebraic) relation between x and y with no arbitrary constants. Euler calls it 'omnino determinata'.

Second class (§50). If Z = Z(x,y,p) and P = Z_p genuinely depends on p, then the equation 0 = N − dP/dx contains second differentials (dp = y'' dx). It is a second-order ODE with two arbitrary constants. Euler concludes that such problems must be posed among curves through two given points. He adds that problems of this class by their nature always demand this restriction, i.e. a fixed-endpoint boundary value problem.

The page thus serves the structural classification. The next page extends the second class to Lagrangians affine in q = y'', i.e. Z + 𝔷(x,y,p)·q, which still give second-order equations. Class III (genuinely q-dependent Z) leads to fourth-order equations.
errors: The image appears to print 'd.(dx/dy)' where the sense requires d.(dy/dx) = dp, the second differential entering dP/dx. This is probably a typographical slip in the original, or a misreading of a damaged print.

Strictly, a second-order equation requires P_p = Z_pp ≠ 0, which Euler expresses loosely as 'P involves p'. That is adequate in context. No mathematical error otherwise: the cancellation giving 0 = N − 𝔐 is correct.

ideas.what: Lagrangians affine in y' give a purely algebraic Euler–Lagrange equation Z_y = 𝔷_x. The term 𝔷p dx is just 𝔷 dy, and if Z_y = 𝔷_x identically the integrand is exact (a null Lagrangian).
ideas.modern_name: degenerate / affine-in-velocity Lagrangians; null Lagrangians (exact forms)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi 1744 already treats integrals reducing to algebraic equations); null Lagrangians systematically studied in the 20th century (Carathéodory and others)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744), ch. 2; Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385); this paper E420

ideas.what: Classification of variational integrals by the order of the Euler–Lagrange equation. Second-order equations carry two constants and so require two fixed endpoints.
ideas.modern_name: order of Euler–Lagrange equations; two-point boundary value problems
ideas.where_published: E65; E385 (Inst. calc. int. III, appendix de calculo variationum)

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard expository material: Euler's classification of variational problems by the order of the Euler–Lagrange equation, including the degenerate affine-in-p case. All of it already appears in Euler's 1744 Methodus and in his integral-calculus textbook (Institutiones calculi integralis, vol. III).
transcription_corrections: The transcribed 'd.(dx/dy)' matches the print, but the intended expression is d.(dy/dx) (= dp). Flag this as a printer's error rather than an OCR error.
In the equation '0 = N − 𝔐' the second symbol is Fraktur 𝔐 (∂𝔷/∂x), correctly rendered.
